summary: Ohio's Port Clinton Light: a stone harbor light of 1833, then the wooden pier light first lit in 1896, now restored and standing in Waterworks Park.

lens.where: lantern room of the restored 1896 tower, installed 2016

structures.note: Split stone, forty feet; razed August 1899
Taken down 1901; replaced by a two-story frame house
Square in plan, octagonal lantern and balcony, on piles at the end of the west pier until 1952; restored and moved to Waterworks Park in 2016
Original built 1902; replica placed beside the tower in 2018

access.note: Tower and grounds in Waterworks Park. Tours on Saturdays noon to 5 p.m., Memorial Day through Labor Day, $3 fee (conservancy).

events.note: Government buys the acreage on the east side of the Portage River mouth from Ezekiel and Charlotte Haines
Split-stone tower, forty feet, with a stone dwelling beside it
Stone tower in service; Austin Smith first keeper
Keeper Austin Smith takes in a shipwrecked party bound for Chicago
Sixth-order Fresnel lens
Light discontinued by the Board (LighthouseFriends)
Reactivated 1 August 1864 with Leander S. Porter as keeper
Discontinued for good; lantern room removed from the stone tower. The conservancy gives 1856 (see resolved_conflicts and notes)
Piers extended into Lake Erie on both sides of the river mouth
Act approved 15 February 1893 authorizes reestablishing the light at a cost not to exceed $1,500; no appropriation yet made
Wooden square pyramidal tower erected on piles at the outer end of the west pier
New light first exhibited 15 July 1896 with a 180-degree lens lantern and ruby chimneys
Old stone tower razed in August 1899; stone carried by steamer Warrington to the Detroit River
Keeper's dwelling replaced by a two-story frame house
Boathouse built for the keeper, who rowed across the river to reach the light
Iron oil house placed on the pier
Oil burners replaced by electricity; light automated
Government sells the lot and keeper's dwelling to a private buyer
Wooden tower removed from the breakwater by Dave Jeremy to his marina on the Portage River; a skeletal tower with a 375 mm lens replaces it
Restoration complete (conservancy; LighthouseFriends announced August 2014)
Ownership signed over to the Port Clinton Lighthouse Conservancy at a ceremony on 14 April 2016 (LighthouseFriends); conservancy home page gives 2012 for the donation
Moved on 16 August 2016 to Waterworks Park
Replica fifth-order Fresnel lens installed 11 September 2016
Replica of the boathouse placed beside the tower

corrections.proposed: tower, wood, pyramidal, built 1896, standing; the 1833 stone tower was razed in 1899
corrections.why: The standing tower is the wooden pier light of 1896, moved to Waterworks Park in 2016. LighthouseFriends and the marker say the stone tower was razed in 1899, so a stone tower of 1833 cannot be the one standing.
The Board's 1896 and 1897 reports give a red light (ruby chimneys); LighthouseFriends and the marker say fixed red.
LighthouseFriends gives a focal plane of 25 feet 8 inches for the 1896 light (about 7.8 m). The USLHS pierhead record gives 25.0 feet. The 10.1 m figure is not supported by any source read.
The tower has belonged to the conservancy since its 2016 transfer, per LighthouseFriends and the conservancy's own pages.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Two towers. The stone light of 1833 (USLHS, marker, conservancy) and the wooden pier light first exhibited in July 1896 (Board reports, LighthouseFriends) are different structures at different spots near the harbor mouth. The 1896 record is for the standing tower.
1870 is the end of the stone light (LighthouseFriends, marker, USLHS). 1952 is the removal of the wooden pier light from the breakwater; the marker says the light continued to operate until 1952.
The stone tower is gone (razed 1899), so the USLHS 'lost' status fits that tower. OpenStreetMap's 'standing' fits the 1896 tower, which was moved to Waterworks Park in 2016.

notes_for_editor: Printed page numbers were not read for any Light-House Board citation; the scan pages are given (the guide's 'scan page' fallback). Check scan 159 and scan 410 in the same volume, annualreportlig02statgoog, which binds the 1896 and 1897 reports: scan 159 holds the 'discontinued some 26 years' sentence and scan 410 the 'first exhibited' sentence and the custodian sentence. Confirm which printed report each falls in. The 1900 (scan 184) and 1899 (scan 209) pages were checked by OCR snippet only. DISAGREEMENTS NOT SETTLED: (a) first discontinuance: conservancy says 1856; LighthouseFriends, USLHS and the marker say 1870; the 1896 report's 'some 26 years' fits about 1870. (b) The Feb 15 act: Board reports say 1893; LighthouseFriends says 1895. (c) Gift of the tower: LighthouseFriends says offered 2011, signed 2016; conservancy home page says donated 2012; conservancy history says owner approached 2010. (d) Lamp count 1833: eight (LighthouseFriends, Platt), 11 to 4 to 5 and 8 (conservancy), 'five 14 Inch reflectors' (USLHS old-station optic field). (e) Range of the 1896 light: six miles (conservancy), eight miles (marker); left out of the record because the unit is statute miles and no sea-range source was read. (f) Focal height: 25 ft 8 in (LighthouseFriends), 25.0 ft (USLHS pierhead), 10.1 m (record, from ENC). (g) Lens order of the 1896 light: fifth order (LighthouseFriends, marker) against the USLHS '6th Order Replica' for the current optic; the 1855 lens was sixth order. (h) Waterfield: first keeper of the new light (LighthouseFriends, USLHS) against 'last keeper of the old stone lighthouse' (conservancy). (i) Oil house: LighthouseFriends says an oil house 'reportedly still remains in the park'; the conservancy says it was removed when the light was electrified in 1926. Left out of the story. POSITION: the record's coordinates are the moved tower in Waterworks Park; USLHS gives the old station at 41.5058, -82.9375, about 1 km away; the 1896 light stood on the west pier. NRHP: no NRHP number is in the record and none was checked. NAMES: Dave Jeremy (1952), Clarence S. Perry, and Wallace Sutherland are named only in their public role as the sources print it; no living-person details beyond that were used. The Hinelines and Captain William Duff are in the prose only (no dates in the sources, so they are not roster lines). Platt's and Pleasonton's words are as LighthouseFriends quotes them; the 1838 and 1843 originals were not read. The Ottawa Union (1870) and the Elmore Independent (1899) are cited only as LighthouseFriends describes them. Chronicling America was searched for Port Clinton lights in Ohio papers 1870-1900; no relevant page turned up. No storm, ice or fog-signal report tied to this light was found in the corpus. The 2016 lens and 2018 boathouse come from LighthouseFriends; the conservancy home page was not checked for newer ownership or access changes after the late-season listing. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28: every quote re-run against its cached source. Board report scan pages re-confirmed with corpus.py page (scan 159 and 410 in annualreportlig02statgoog; scan 193 is the Port Clinton entry of the 1893 report, printed p.144 per the Board's index; scan 209 for 1899; scan 184 for 1900). Printed pages still not read. Story changed in this check: 'offered' changed to 'donated' (LighthouseFriends' word, 2011); lens crafter now named as Artworks Florida (Dan Spinella stays out of the prose); the Ottawa Union proposal reworded to the source's 'maintain'; the 2010 owner's aim put in the conservancy's words (transfer to city ownership, not 'giving it back'); the late-October tour inference removed; the marker's reason given as 'poor location'; Platt's chimney exception added. The marker's 'keeper's dwelling and boathouse have not survived' is kept in the marker's words.
